maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 22 I spoke to this House of the enthusiasm, imagination and creativity of the younger generation as so abundantly demonstrated in the quality and quantity of the proposals submitted under the Opportunities for Youth program.
Last week, as agreed, I began to announce both to the students and the public at large what projects had been approved. To date, some 600 project co-ordinators have been notified that their projects will be financed by the government of Canada. Similar announcements are being made at the rate of some one hundred a day. As I already mentioned to the House, we hope to have this phase of the program completed around mid-May. To date, we have received more than 13,000 projects.
On April 22, I emphasized that the government would respond to the enthusiasm of youth and I am pleased to announce today that the government has decided to allocate $10 million more to the Opportunities for Youth program. The government is aware that the amount does not fully meet the young people's requests but we are convinced that the vast majority of the many excellent proposals may now be approved. Furthermore, we count on being able to inform the young people whose projects may now be approved through this additional amount by May 25 at the latest. The Opportunities for Youth program, it will be remembered, Mr. Speaker, is based on the initiative of the young people and is designed to create new jobs and additional activities.
The government has presented a program to which the youth of our country has spontaneously responded. It is therefore obvious that the program truly meets the needs of the younger generation.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I must congratulate the Secretary of State for accepting the suggestions made on this side of the House and elsewhere.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Hon. members over there have a short memory. I am glad that the government is expanding the funds for the program from $15 million to $25 million. As happens so often when the government finally accepts the advice of the opposition, its action is too little and too late.
Some hon. Membersr Oh, oh!

Opportunities for Youth Program

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Quite obviously the vast majority of young people who took the government at its word when the program was first announced will still be disappointed. They are already disappointed because in most cases they have not received any information about the projects they submitted almost one month ago. The fact that the government is now accepting projects at the rate of 100 a day will be cold satisfaction to the vast majority of young people who hoped and expected the government to respond favourably to their applications.
Although all hon. members welcome the addition of $10 million to the program, I must say that some of us are extremely disappointed that the Secretary of State has not indicated what alternative suggestions or proposals he or his department has in mind with respect to the remaining thousands of projects. After all, some 13,000 projects have been submitted. If about 600 have already been accepted, and a few hundred more may be accepted, this means that between 11,000 and 12,000 projects will go unanswered. This is one of the most, if not the most, shocking aspects of the whole Opportunities for Youth program.
I would have been much happier if the Secretary of State had indicated that he and his officials, in light of the great reaction to this program, were now actively consulting with municipalities, provinces, universities and industry so that some of the most imaginative projects that have been put forward by Canada's young people could be acted upon either in the private sector or in other areas of the public sector. Instead we have been told that, while an additional $10 million will be allocated to the program, the vast majority of projects, conceived in good faith and presented to the minister and his officials with great hopes, will simply not be allowed to come to fruition. That is simply not good enough for the hundreds of thousands of this country's young people who have taken the time and trouble to advance some of the most important, useful and constructive projects that young people of this country have advanced for many years. I urge the minister, in conjunction with his officials, to give serious consideration within the coming week to finding areas where programs that have not been accepted may yet be instituted in order to give our young people an opportunity to serve and so that they may be assisted to continue their education in the fall.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
on behalf of this party may I thank the minister for making his statement and announcing that an extra $10 million is to be made available for the Opportunities for Youth program. Like the hon. member for Egmont, I am very happy to see that the minister has acted upon our suggestions-

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
-and upon the suggestions of thousands of young people across the country. The issue that must be raised is that this announcement has been made on May 11, two or three weeks after many university stu-

dents have finished their classes, when it should have been made several months ago. I do not see why we should still be formulating student employment policies in the month of May. I do not see why this had to happen. It should have been done last fall or in the early winter so that the young people could have planned their university years and their summers.
As the minister has said, thousands of projects will not be granted or approved. What will happen to the young people depending on getting jobs through the Opportunities for Youth program when their projects are turned down on May 25? How much time will they have to compete for jobs that may not be available? These are things the minister should have thought of early last fall and early last winter instead of coming up with an ill-planned ad hoc type of Opportunities for Youth program at the last moment.
There are other points which come to mind. How many jobs will actually be created under this program? We still do not know the answer. In the jobs that are created how long will the students be employed? Will they only be employed for six or seven weeks or for two or three months? Many students need full summer employment if they are to be able to return to university next fall. They also need summer jobs that pay wages high enough to enable them to continue their studies. These are some of the questions which the program has failed to answer.
In general, this program is a good public relations job, but how much of the problem will it really solve? I would like to make two or three suggestions.
The minister and his department should start thinking right now about next year and do some long-range planning. Why not convene a conference with young people such as the proposed conference that was cancelled last spring? Why not contact the provincial and municipal governments with regard to planning for next year? This should have been done this year instead of this last minute attempt to put forward a patched-up program.
The government should also be pursuing a policy of full employment. If we had full employment we would not be faced with so many problems in finding jobs for our young people.
Finally, whether a student finds a summer job should not determine whether he returns to university. We must think about universal accessibility to education regardless of one's financial background.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
One's future in education should not depend on how successful one is in competing for jobs that are all too scarce in Canada today.
These are a few points that I hope the minister and the government will consider. Let us not get into this bind next year and disappoint the students again by coming out with a plan at the last moment. Young people want to do something. The minister was surprised that the young people have responded so enthusiastically to this program. I was not surprised. I knew the young people wanted to do something, so let us start planning now for next year and get on with something meaningful.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-INCREASE IN FUNDS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last March 16, the right hon. Prime Minister invited our young people to participate actively in the Opportunities for Youth program.
On April 22, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) cited some statistics and pointed out, for instance, that his department had received 2,485 projects and that he was not surprised because the young were enthused over the opportunity of working towards building the country.
Today, the Secretary of State announced in the House that he had received over 13,000 projects from students and that of this number, only 600 had been approved so far. He announced also that the total budget of the program would be increased by $10 million.
No matter what members opposite might want to say, I would like to remind them that after the announcement made by the Secretary of State which has been reported on page 5150, I strongly urged the government to increase the program's budget, so as not to augment further the feeling of frustration of Canadian students.
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to take this opportunity to direct your attention to the ambivalence of the problem confronting the young students of Canada, namely to complete their studies while trying to avoid as much as possible running into debts. It is a well known fact that the scholarship and loan system contributes directly to get them into debt and to delay their start in life and the benefits that their knowledge and skills can bring to society. When they get out of school, students are up to here in debt and receive no government help to continue their education while governments claim credit for making education free.
Moreover, young people are impatient to participate in building their country in projects where their personal initiative is emphasized, where development, environment beautification, recreation, pollution control are involved. These are problems that are of deep concern to young Canadians and their response to the Opportunities for Youth program-more than 13,000 projects probably involving thousands of students-shows the number of students who are in debt and neglected by governments and also their interest not so much in dissent-since they know that in any case the government will not give them a hearing-as in building up their country.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express somewhat qualified praise of the Secretary of State for the budget and for the number of projects presented by students which have been approved. Ten million dollars are certainly better than the total of $14.7 million originally allotted for the whole program, but that certainly is still inadequate.
Therefore, I want to renew my pleading with the government and particularly the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State to review their positions and further increase the budget in order that the Opportunities for Youth program should not bring about increased frustration among students who, believe it or not are really people to build up our country.

speechtext:
That this House believes that an enlightened program of human and economic progress for northern Canada offers great opportunities for the people of this country; and that the economic and social policies of the present government have brought about confusion and delayed progress; and that it is essential to make appropriate changes in our approach in respect of northern Canada;
And this House condemns the government for its failure to promote a truly Canadian strategy for the north based on human, capital and natural resources, and urges that appropriate policies be adopted at once that will bring about such development in that region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when you started reading the motion I saw that there were in the House three of the four horsemen on the government side who have been riding off in different directions on this issue over the last two or three months but three of the horsemen have vanished, leaving only the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). I had hoped that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis)-soon, we hope, to be given the accolade of minister of the environment-the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) and of course last, but not by any means least, the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) would have remained for the debate. I am in great hopes that the latter hon. member, before this debate concludes, may give us the benefit of his views, although he may well have left that opportunity to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who is here and who may well be informed on this particular issue.
This party, which has the honour to be Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, may not have any copyright on issues dealing with the north but certainly by right of its history, traditions and actions, it has the best right to bring forward a motion of this kind. The first leader of this party after confederation was one of the main architects of national unity. He brought in a program and a national policy which has continued to the present time.
During my period in this House and during the elections in 1957 and 1958 the party, then led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), pro-
May 11, 1971

posed a program of northern development which caught the imagination of this country and which was to a large extent implemented during the period when that government was in office. It was the Conservative party which built the railroads that stitched together the far flung areas of the northern continent. When we talk about a country which is unique we use the words bilingualism, multiculturalism, diversity and economic conditions. I suggest to you and to this House, Mr. Speaker, that there is a quality of uniqueness about a country which has a large and well established industrial base, a great expanse of territory and a frontier land awaiting human development to bring about the coalition of forces involved in a nation of this kind.
In spite of differences of language, manners and customs, and in spite of things silently gone out of mind and of things violently destroyed, this land should bind together in passion and understanding and shared problems, a great empire of human society. From time to time this party has been the instrument to bring out to some substantial extent this form of development.
In 1957 and 1958 there was a Road to Resources program; there was the construction of a railroad line into the northern territories, something which had been talked about for many years but was implemented by this party; there was construction of airports and airstrips throughout the north; there were a number of factors which brought about facilities in northern Canada which had been lacking in the past. In his concern for the questions relating to northern development as they touch upon industrial development in other parts of Canada and the dangers of pollution, the present leader of this party has seen fit to intervene and to inspect personally some of the problems of the north and to talk to its people. While he has had some opportunities to discuss this in the House, I am sure we will have an opportunity to hear more about it.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to this House that our party is qualified by experience and desire to deal With this particular problem. On the other hand, the government is made up of a party which, from the earliest days, has scoffed, jeered and poured contempt on programs leading to northern development. The records of this House are studded with illustrations of my statement. Defences are like trousers; they should be kept up at all times. Unfortunately, the government's defences in this area are down, and there has been a most improper and indecent exposure of the government's insignificant and irrelevant programs with regard to northern development. History shows that this government and the Liberal party have scuttled the expansion of genuine Canadian development. I will not go into the facts; they are well known and taught in the history books. Children in school know that the Liberal party has never been interested in northern development.

speechtext:
I am afraid that they were joined in opposition by my friends to my left, who were then members of the CCF party. They voted against the bill incorporating the Pine Point railway. The Conservative government of the day, supported by its Conservative members, instituted and brought forward in this country the very wise and sensible program of railway development which has brought about such great improvement in our northern country.
My hon. friends opposite, both while in government and in opposition, have also been opposed to certain other programs. The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) illustrated, with his eloquent and articulate remarks, the dangers inherent in the Yukon minerals legislation and in the bill dealing with the Northern Canada Power Commission. This afternoon, in the question period, the Bennett dam was mentioned. Although I and members of my party protested the building of this dam to the Liberal government of the day, that Liberal government insisted upon proceeding with that dam in the face of what I suggest were definite warnings about dangers which were inherent in the proposal to construct that dam. Its construction was bound to affect seriously all those who inhabited the downstream areas in Alberta and in the Northwest Territories. The government insisted on going ahead. They would not demand from the government of British Columbia, as it was their moral and legal duty to do, assurances that that government would proceed to secure a permit under the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act for the building of that dam. This would have meant that the government of British Columbia would have had to file documents indicating what its engineering plans were. I am convinced that if that information had been made available to the public, the people of Canada and this party would have brought pressure on the government of British Columbia because they would have realized the necessity of taking steps to prevent the serious deterioration of the environment which has affected the people of northern Alberta and of the Northwest Territories.

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada
The Liberal government has dragged its feet continuously on the question of self-government for the Yukon and for the Northwest Territories. They are satisfied, as they have always been, to maintain the status quo, meaning a quasi-colonial establishment.
May I turn to the motion in my name. After all, I could spend 30 minutes cataloguing the sins, errors and omissions of this government. I want to speak constructively and to make some proposals which I hope the government will consider, although I have strong doubts about that. I want to touch briefly on certain areas covered by the motion and leave to my colleagues the task of going into them in more detail later. We must re-examine the form in which we deliver our resources outside of Canada's borders. Canadian needs of the future must be examined and taken into consideration when considering the question of our resources. We must consider dangers to the environment involved in the processing of our resources in northern Canada and in the use of our rivers, waters, minerals, natural gas and petroleum. We must consider the extent to which we can make use of a combination of our resources to produce power. We must also consider the best way to use resources which we have in large quantities. I am talking about resources which may be refined and processed in this country. For far too long there has been no meeting of minds on this issue. I hope that the hon. member for Duvernay who has made public comments on these matters will enlarge on his views in this debate.
I am convinced that in certain situations we ought to rationalize certain industries. It will be possible for the people of this country to process and refine, in secondary and tertiary industries, resources obtained and developed in the north. All this will require careful planning. We will need to examine our resources and catalogue them. We will need to decide where the markets are for these and, having decided whether the markets are to be in Canada or outside or both inside and outside of Canada, we must decide where we can best process these resources. If we can best process some of these resources in Canada, we must consider our ability to deliver some of these resources to countries outside Canada. This, in turn, will lead to the consideration of transportation questions. Too often we have blindly worked out schemes of transportation to apply in northern Canada without calculating carefully what we ought to transport and where we ought to transport it. Careful planning of that sort will be absolutely essential.
There must be, therefore, a rational approach to the exploring and to the cataloguing of our resources, and a rational approach to our consideration of markets, to our consideration of the placing, processing and refining of these resources, and to our consideration of transportation questions. We have heard much about transportation from this government; yet all too often, when rhetoric is mated with a Liberal government, we find that it produces only masterly inactivity. Some of my colleagues will deal with the question of the TAPS line, the question of using the Mackenzie valley for pipelines, the dangers inherent in that course and what precautions

must be taken before that route may be used if there is an economic need to use it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made a few comments on this matter. Yet his comments have been of the kind that make his silences positively delightful, Mr. Speaker.
However, I want to deal mainly with the question of the native peoples of the country, and the extent to which they are enabled to develop their individuality, something which has been lost in much of our society. With regard to the native peoples, Mr. Speaker, the attitude of this government is abysmal. In particular, I refer to the refusal of this government to accept the fact that the people of the Northwest Territories and other parts of Canada have aboriginal rights. I do not have the time to deal with this as extensively as I would like, but I want to refer the House to the royal proclamation of 1763. I am going to analyse and summarize that document very briefly in so far as it deals with aboriginal rights.
This royal proclamation made it abundantly clear that the Indian people of Canada, including western and northwestern Canada, have specific aboriginal rights with regard to their properties, including the land, forests and minerals under the land. That was made quite plain. As a matter of fact, in one or two judgments the late Mr. Justice Sissons of the territorial court of the Northwest Territories referred to this proclamation and the rights of the aboriginal people. He made it abundantly clear in his judgments that these rights have never been surrendered.
We have a situation today where the government is talking about mineral rights in the north, the possibility of pipelines down the Mackenzie valley and development of the north. I suggest to hon. members that a condition precedent to acts of this nature must be the negotiation and settlement of the aboriginal rights of the native people of the north. I wish to add on this particular score that the history of the dealings of the English speaking people throughout the world with native people, while it is in part a record which is not universally good, nevertheless has always been one of practicing understanding of the native people. This practice has acquired the status of a tradition, almost a law, by which the natives have rights. The lands belong to them until they are taken away by act of Parliament or negotiation. This course was followed in so far as the lands between the west shore of Lake Superior and the Rocky mountains were concerned. A number of treaties were entered into. Those treaties were specifically enacted for the purpose of acquiring the rights and title to those lands from the Indian people. Concessions were made, although they were most inadequate. These treaties were never honoured. The people of this country have this on their conscience and they should be concerned about it. At least, in those cases, the government went through the form of executing a treaty.
For a large part of the Northwest Territories, there are absolutely no treaties. The minister shakes his head. I admit that one of the treaties did cover the southern
May 11, 1971

part of the Mackenzie district, but that treaty was nego-ciated outside of the territories. At that time there was not the distinction that exists today between the territories and the provinces. Because of that, the treaty included some of the areas of northern Canada.
If pipelines are built in the Mackenzie valley, they will be built under circumstances which at the present time do not take into account the legal and moral rights of the native people of northern Canada. That is the smallest part of the problem. What about the rights of these people to the minerals, lands and forests? I suggest it will lay heavy upon the consciences of the Canadian people, including the members of this House, if this pipeline is constructed before negotiations being entered into take place with the natives. This problem will be settled only when there have been conferences and discussions, not the kind of consultation in which we say to the Indian people that this is what we are going to give them. There should be prior, reasonable consultations and ultimate agreement. If we do not do this, we will have something on our consciences for a great many years.

I wish to quote a statement made by John Buchan at the time of the commencement of World War II. At that time he visited the Peace River in his capacity as Governor General. I had an opportunity to show him some of the places of historical interest, including the place where Alexander MacKenzie spent the winter of 1791. He intended to write a historical novel dealing with the north, but death intervened. I wish to quote a statement he made shortly before his death. He talked about the Peace River pioneer. This statement can now be widened to cover the pioneers all over the north. I quote:
He is wholly secure, he possesses his soul, he is the true philosopher. He is one of the few aristocrats left in the world. He

has a right sense of the values of life because his cosmos embraces both nature and man. I think he is the most steadfast human being now alive.

speechtext:
No, no, Mr. Speaker. We repress the individual at our peril, and we tamper with him to our great danger. We erect monolithic and gigantic imitations of the prehistory hunting band, the earliest example of the human herd, which are dedicated to the initiation and enlargement of the welfare state. In the end, we will find, as we are beginning to find now, that no such state can continue to exist without some form of police power to enforce conformity.
I do not know whether the exception will always prove the rule, but certainly it has been our experience as a nation that men at war, fighting for survival, will tighten their social contract, renounce individual demands, and exist as a single group. The quality of the group, not the distinction of the individual, then becomes a criterion for survival. Thinking of the individual as the product of the north and the north as a place which can generate individualism as we used to know it, some people conceive of the individual as the ancient reality and society as the human invention. I cannot accept this. It seems that the social order, with its rules and regulations, alphas and omegas, territories and hierarchies, has been the evolutionary way. Surely, it was the individual who created our civilization. It was certainly the individual who created the north. He went in there on his own and created what we have at the present time. This can be seen if we look back over closely recorded history and check out the contributions which have been made. For this reason in many parts of this country, certainly the north, we must make elbow room for individuality.
I realize that it is fashionable today to accept violence, aggression, crime and related phenomena as the product of the individual. There is a limited element of truth in this. However, when we examine our history, are we not entitled to say that the aggressive self-assertive tendencies in the emotional life of the individual are less dangerous to the species than the integrative tendencies of group society? Certainly, the number of victims of individual crimes committed in any given period of history cannot be compared to the masses who have been sacrificed in the name of a religion, a dynasty or a political system. And so, while we desire to redirect our trinking to provide far a better use of our resources, to deal with the question of taxation so that taxation may be used as an instrument of incentive, not as a weapon to blunt the initiative of individuals in the north, while we wish to establish a blueprint for development leading to a greater use of manpower in the processing and refining of our resources, and while provision must be made for consequential transportation facilities, to my mind the human resources which can be accommodated and shaped on the anvil of the north, rank highest, for it is

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada toward a reacknowledgment of the virtues of individualism that the north must be adopted.

speechtext:
I want to take an entirely different road from that followed by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) because I do not believe the situation we find in the north today is the result of action by this government alone. It is just as much the result of a vision which the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had some years ago, and what he tried to do. Indeed, it is the result of decades of a certain type of approach to the north.
What disturbs members of my party is not so much some of the details involved in this approach as the fact that the traditional attitude to the resources of the north has been the same as has been shown toward the resources houth of the north, if I may put that way, namely, a greedy and reckless desire for exploitation, a greedy and reckless depletion of non-renewable resources for very little purpose other than to ship them out of this country, mainly to the United States. In all of this development in the north, there has been no evidence of any intention to build communities. There has been no adequate concern shown for the native population over the years, and I am not singling out the present minister or the present government. There has been no adequate concern shown for the environment, no adequate concern for the future of Canada, that is whether or not some day we may need the resources we are now so anxious to yank out of the ground. There has been no adequate concern shown for the needs of the world, really. We simply cannot wait to exploit these non-renewable resources and sell them to the one country in the world which uses up by far the largest proportion of the planet's natural resources, necessarily to the disadvantage of newly emerging countries who will need them badly in a little while. And we are doing this without any thought, it would appear, for its effect on the increasingly serious problem of foreign ownership in this country.
The wealth with which we have been endowed, not only in the Yukon and Northwest Territories but in regions to the south, is now to be recklessly exploited by large corporations with financial assistance from the government, to no social purpose which is evident to anyone who has studied this subject-and I have studied it a little. Why are the government and the Official Opposition so anxious that all this exploration for oil, minerals and gas should take place?

Does anyone in the government, or even the department, know what is the long range plan? Is it intended that the population in the north should be increased, and if so are plans being made for that situation? Is it intended that the native people are to be employed? If so, are they to be suitably trained? Is it intended that the resources which are exploited should be used for any other purpose than shipment south of the Canadian border? In the course of a fair amount of reading in the last 24 hours I have been unable to discover any long range plan. It appears we are simply anxious to invite every corporation in a position to do so to accept the benefits and incentives provided by the government, to enter the north, endanger the environment and do all the other things I have mentioned, without purpose in terms of the future of this country or, indeed, the future welfare of the world.
Take the question of concern for the natives. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) rightly insisted that one of the first things to be done is to settle the claims of the native people in the northern regions. It seems clear that they have rights to the land and its resources. Some machinery must be set up to deal with these claims, and not merely a committee to discuss them, but a body authorized to take steps to settle them. As the minister well knows, both the House of Representatives and the Senate of the United States have bills before them at the present time in connection with this subject. I believe they are now in the hands of the joint committee whose function it is to reconcile legislation introduced in each of the two houses. These bills seem to suggest payments to the natives of Alaska amounting to well over $1 billion besides large tracts of land which would be granted to them for the future. But I have heard no suggestion that consideration is to be given to aboriginal rights of native people in the Canadian north.
In turn, now, to consider our record as employers in the north. I cannot see how the minister or anyone else in Canada can help feeling ashamed of this. We must not forget that government departments are very large employers of labour.
I used the term the other day in another context "mincing steps of progress" in regard to our native people. By now we ought to have taken giant steps of progress. Every time we pick up a report by a member of the minister's department, a journalist, student, professor or what have you, who has made a survey of the situation we see the same situation, namely that the use of native people in the exploitation of our resources in the north has been very small indeed. Have we made a study of the need for all these minerals, oil and gas that we are now looking for in the north? Are these reserves required in Canada or elsewhere outside of the United States of America? Has anyone made a study to make certain what would happen 5, 10, or 20 years from now if we had these reserves for sale at that time when the needs of the United States will be a great deal more
stringent and the needs of the other parts of the world will be serious? Have we made any study at all? I suggest to you that we have not. We have a large tract of land with which this country is blessed. Everyone expects there are large reserves of minerals, oil, gas and other riches, so, we simply invite people to break open the land and pull out the resources without any plan or study whatsoever.
The hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) was saying things which I think I could claim, without any arrogance, our party has been claiming for many years now.

speechtext:
I want to say to the hon. member for Duvernay that he is right when he points out to us that large amounts of capital are now being sunk into mineral, oil and gas exploration and exploitation and are being wasted. The only real justification for going at these resources now in any part of Canada, particularly the part over which this government has jurisdiction, is to build around these resources complete industrial complexes. We should not only take the resources out of the land, we should be building processing, smelting and refining plants, and building within reasonable economic distance necessary secondary and tertiary manufacturing plants, so that around these resources in Canada's land we are building all the various industrial complexes for which the resources should be used.
In that way only can we build communities up north that are viable and lasting. In that way only can we have a permanent type of security for the native people and the other people who make their homes in the north, and in that way only can we have what the hon. member for Peace River was talking about, the development of more of the individualism he suggests the north produces. I am sure he is right. In this way only can we attract more people up there. This is the only way we can build cities in the north of greater size, of viability and lasting usefulness to the people concerned rather than little cities populated with hippies as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested some time ago. That was a pretty meaningless and typical Prime Ministerial statement, or the kind of statement made by this Prime Minister.
Merely to pull the riches out of the ground and ship them away to the United States, as we do now, will mean that not only are we shipping our resources out, we are shipping thousands of jobs out of this country. We are making it impossible for this country to develop the larger industrial requirements which can meet the needs of the world as well as of Canada. We are making it impossible to plan for the real development of the north

May 11, 1971

which needs population as well as drills, machines and equipment. If you are not concerned about building the north with people, then of course these corporations will do it for you. They do not need very many people to pull the riches out of the ground and ship them out. That does not require very many people. That does require, as pointed out by the hon. member for Duvernay, very large capital but not many workers.
If we are thinking of developing and building the north in community terms, not only for the native people and other people who are there, but for the people who can be attracted from the crowded cities in the south because of a particular kind of life that many people in the south might prefer, then we are talking of the kind of planning I have been suggesting. That kind of planning will not take place if we merely hold out carrots to the large private corporations, well over half of which are foreign-owned. More than 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the area involved is being exploited by foreign-owned corporations, mainly from the United States, although not exclusively so.
This will all require public investment, public control and public planning. It will require the kind of Canada development corporation the NDP has proposed, with a large funding that the minister and his associates could then use if they had the imagination and the will to do so. They could then develop the riches in the north for the benefit of Canada, the Canadian people and for the development of much larger populations in decent, modern communities in the north. It is only in this way we will get to the point of moving self-government for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories out of the talking stage and into reality.

I would not say touche at all. I was going to say something rather silly but perhaps I should not. If I exchanged positions with the hon. member I feel certain I would be better off, but I do not know anything about him and he knows nothing about me. I have not been practising labour law since I was re-elected in 1965, except in little driblets, so my friend does not have to worry about that.
In short, let me repeat what I commenced to say and then I will sit down. Our concern is not merely with the details, which will be pointed out during the debate and have been pointed out already, but with the general approach to the subject. We are concerned about the reckless and greedy exploitation of resources without any plan for the north, the native people there or for Canada as a whole. Let me express my convictions that five years from now, when a debate on this subject takes place, we will say the same things about each other because, relatively speaking, the position will still be that the large private corporations will be making a killing out of the north and that the native people and others in the north, as in many other parts of Canada, will be getting very little in return for the exploitation of Canada's rich resources. I therefore plead with the minister that he pay some attention to the over-all long-term program, and tell the House and the people of Canada whether he is merely interested in depleting the resources or that he and his government are interested in building a permanent series of communities where Canadians can live in comfort, dignity and in pride.
Therefore, in order to make clear what we have in mind and in view of the fact that I find it a little difficult to understand precisely what kind of policy the mover of the motion had in mind, I move:
That the motion he amended by deleting all the words after the words "that appropriate policies be adopted" and by substituting therefor the following words:
"which would take into account environmental dangers, the problem of foreign ownership, the future needs of Canada, and the basic and prior rights of the native inhabitants of the Territories, including their claim for a settlement that would recognize their rights in the land of its resources".
I move this amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), because the motion as proposed merely talks about bringing about such development in that region, without enumerating the elements which are of importance. We thought it would be useful to set out the elements the policy ought to have.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ADOPT POLICIES TO DEVELOP THE HUMAN, CAPITAL AND NATURAL RESOURCES OF NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our country's wealth, importance and size offer us in fact endless possibilities. We are all aware of the huge potential of these vast territories in Northern Canada. Unfortunately, it is quite true that the present government has spread

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada confusion and delayed progress as is mentioned in the motion now before us.
Hesitations and delays have jeopardized the successful start of development in this vast region. It even seemed, at one time, that our powerful neighbours to the South were enjoying so much powers that the very unity of our territory could be involved.
So I agree with the non confidence motion which in part reads as follows:
-condemns the government for its failure to promote a truly Canadian strategy for the North based on human capital and natural resources,-
As long as we fail to apply the basic and elementary principles of a sound economy, we will always meet with difficulties of all kinds which too often become insuperable obstacles.
The appropriate programs which would cause such a development to take place in that area, as recommended in the motion, cannot be but of an economic character.
Needless to say, I take into consideration the preservation of the rights and privileges of the native Indians and Eskimos, this being but one aspect of the overall respect for the human individual.
But, Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I shall dwell a little longer on the economic aspect of the problem raised by northern development. An adequate financial policy would first determine the true viable potential, taking into account the existing natural resources and the human resources required for this development. The actual potential or actual credit of the area could be determined and converted into banking credit by way of our own Bank of Canada.
If we could start off from this elementary principle of issuing the credit we need to develop whatever is physically apt to be developed, most of the difficulties would dissolve. We have been saying for years and we are still saying more forcibly and vehemently than ever that for us the time has come to take a hard look at the possibility of placing credit in the service of Canada's development and particularly in the service of the development of these immense undeveloped regions which constitute the Canadian north. These areas could contribute greatly to the welfare and progress of all Canadians.
It would therefore be important to try precisely to use interest-free loans from the Bank of Canada for the development of these tremendous natural resources of the great northern territory, which are either underground or lying on the surface.
Mr. Speaker, one cannot object, in my opinion, that this is the same old story, and that we think we can solve all problems by saying: Let us use the Bank of Canada!
Mr. Speaker, when something is true, even if its authenticity and profitability have never been fully tested, it remains true, and we can always think better of it, at a given time, and apply it as we would wish, as an increasing proportion of the Canadian people would wish.
So, Mr. Speaker, if we eliminate this problem of capital investment, as far as northern development is concerned, by using the credit possibilities of the Bank of Canada, we could give more time to the consideration of programs, engineering works and their consequences on the native population of these areas. We could, in other words, carry out much more profitable, efficient and humane work, if we were not so concerned with that big problem of capital investment.
We are all aware to some extent, as I said a while ago, of the development possibilities in the Far North, especially of the inexhaustible oil resources. However, we would have again to consider the development of those oil resources in a way that would benefit the citizens of this country. One overriding concern should dictate every agreement and progress in this regard, namely that it must be really useful not only to the people of these regions, but to all Canadians, and this constant care which should be ours, would, in my opinion, allow for the harmonious development of these regions, for the greatest pride and the greatest good of all people in this country.
The development of all the other mineral resources, the importance of which is not exactly known to us, might result in a true expansion which could only please all Canadians.
The motion now before us, says that the government has failed in its task in this regard, and I think we have to admit that it is quite true. I do not understand why we have all sorts of designated areas in Canada where grants are available and yet the program does not apply north of the sixtieth parallel. Just what did that former cabinet minister say in his letter of resignation, as submitted to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? Among other things, he is reported to have said, "Canada is fortunate in its resource base and can insist on exports with a higher labour content. Tax concessions that force the pace of our raw material exports or favour the over-employment of capital, which we have to import, at the expense of labour, which is in surplus, would not be consistent with long run Canadian growth and employment objectives." "If Canada is to be an industrial force in the 1980's" he said, "we must be prepared now to husband our resources and to select those areas in which we can be internationally competitive and to manage and invest in the resources, physical and human, that will give us a compelling position." Those are strong words, Mr. Speaker, and it is evident that the former minister is of the opinion that Canadian economic policy is directed too heavily towards the export of resources. He is also concerned that present government tax policies favour investment in new machinery rather than the creation of jobs.
In my view there is nothing wrong with tax policies which favour investment in new machinery, since any company seeking to establish itself in the north must undertake additional expenses. At the same time, however, our tax laws should be amended to encourage new

job opportunities through the processing and manufacturing of our raw materials.
It would be difficult to speak on this motion without commenting on the $6 billion hydroelectric project for James Bay recently announced by the Premier of Quebec. This will be the biggest financial undertaking in Quebec's history; yet to date no one has been told how the project will be financed or where the power will be sold. The financial implications of this project are far reaching. I say this because the proposed development will be the largest hydroelectric project ever to be undertaken in North America, and it will have to be financed almost entirely by foreign capital. All Canadians are concerned about the proposed inflow of foreign capital in such large amounts, since that could place further pressures on our dollar. That, in turn, would be harmful to Canada's export oriented manufacturing industry. While it is true that the James Bay project will provide thousands of construction jobs, there is concern about the over-al impact of this project on our economy and on our national unemployment problem. Hopefully, this hydroelectric project, when developed, will encourage the processing of more raw materials in Canada, will encourage new manufacturing industries in northern Quebec and will encourage increased productivity at lower cost, for only increased productivity and the economic benefits that it brings will ease our serious unemployment problem.
How serious is this problem, Mr. Speaker? Last month there were some 625,000 Canadians unemployed, representing about 8 per cent of the Nation's labour force. In March, the nation's consumer price index reached 131.3 points, an increase of 1.9 per cent over the index at the same time last year. Spelled out in layman's language, this means that something which cost $100 ten years ago now costs $131.30. Surely, someone in this government could stop long enough between trips from Canada to some foreign country to ask these questions:	what
brought about this situation? Why have we so many people unemployed? Why has our cost of living reached such fantastic heights? If someone were to ask these questions I feel certain that the answers would be that the government has established wrong policies in the wrong places at the wrong times, and that the Liberal party has been following this course since 1965.
The sad truth is that in this period in which the Liberal party has been in power, Canada has had too much inflation, unemployment and slow growth. Our existing economic policies are not adequately coping with our national needs and problems. These are not my views alone, Mr. Speaker. They are also the views of Mr. John Young, the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission, who told the Star Forum, as reported in the Toronto Daily Star of March 10, that the country's present level of unemployment results from the inflation which was allowed to develop and persist between 1965 and 1968 and the inability of the experts to agree on a way to cope with it. Who are the experts today, Mr. Speaker? Mr. John Young is one of them. Although he obviously
May 11, 1971

does not have any of the answers, it appears that neither he nor his staff of bureaucrats have any intention of giving up their jobs, thereby taking the load of their salaries and expenses off the back of the Canadian taxpayer.
When the Progressive Conservative party was in power, we had a policy of northern development. We called it Roads to Resources. What did the Liberals say? They called it a policy of building roads from igloo to igloo. They scoffed and they jeered. Obviously, the Liberal party has never been overconcerned with the development of our northern resources. Ottawa's bureaucrats have shown some interest in the north, but they want absolute control over this area so that they can conduct a vast experiment in state socialism. If this ever happens, all initiative, ambition and development will be destroyed. At the present time we have an example of this condition in our nation. We see the incentive of our people destroyed and all of Canada fast becoming subservient to the state.
Anyone who serves on the Standing Committee on Public Accounts has a better understanding why Canada and bureaucratic Ottawa is in such a mess. I have been here since 1957. For most of those years I have served on the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. I have learned that when a departmental head makes a real booboo, he is not dismissed or demoted. He is, of course, moved, but he will most likely be promoted to serve as the assistant deputy in an old department or possibly as the head of a new department whose activities are only adding to our inflationary problems.
Canada and the present Liberal government are prisoners of these appointed bureaucrats. By the time one of these mandarins has worked his way to the top or accepted a top position, as did Mr. Pickersgill, he has lost touch with the people and the country. Money is no longer the taxpayers' hard-earned dollars, it is something to be spent, and always a little more than was budgeted so that the budget can be increased the next year.

speechtext:
Programs are set up, not in terms of what they will do for the people but on the basis of what they will do for the department. This results in continuous infighting among departments for control over certain programs. We recently had an obvious example of this when no less than seven departments were fighting over which would be responsible for administering control over pollution. The Department of Fisheries won the battle.
As a result of this victory, the Department of Fisheries is to be abolished. In the eyes of some civil servants, it is obviously not important. It is to be replaced with the department of the environment which will have approximately 13,000 employees. As no existing building in Ottawa is large enough to house this enormous staff, the mandarins have decided that a new, modern, large building will be built in Hull. While this is being done, the Department of Public Works will build a new bridge
Development of Northern Canada
from Ottawa to Hull so that the employees can get to and from work on time.
I have no objection to the building being erected in Hull. What I am trying to point out is that Parliament and its elected representatives were never consulted about this development. In fact, when the decision was made to build the new bridge, it was evident from the loud outcries that there had been no consultation with Ottawa city council, Hull city council or the provincial highways departments of Ontario and of Quebec. This was simply a bureaucrat's dream. In their opinion, what the bureaucrats can dream the taxpayers can afford. Once they have made their plans, it is useless to try to interfere. Outside advice is not wanted or tolerated. For example, look at the number of recommendations of the Glassco Royal Commission on government efficiency which never saw the light of day. What happened to the Carter Royal Commission Report on Taxation? Was it completely useless? When it came time for a task force to study Canada's welfare programs, who headed the task force? It was none other than the deputy minister of Health and Welfare who brought most of the old programs into being. Was he going to say that there was a better way?
During a discussion over loans to the CBC in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts last week, Mr. Reisman, the deputy minister of Finance, said that Parliament had approved the loans so they were the responsibility of Parliament. Parliament only hears of these over expenditures by the CBC after they are a fait accompli.
I have said enough to indicate that, in my opinion, some of the rights of Parliament must be restored. If Parliamentarians are to be held responsible to their electorate, a way must be found to give them some voice in the decision making process for it is the decisions ore-sently being made by people who are not responsible to the taxpayers of Canada which in no small way have contributed to the present crisis in our economy and our society.
In my opinion, our economy is in a mess as a result of the clumsy, ham-handed policies of the present government as set out by one of the cabinet's "yes men", namely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). Here is a' man whose left hand does not know what his right hand is doing. He is so lacking in mental intellect and moral fibre that he continues to support the left wing policies of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), the three men who rule cabinet and therefore Canada, when his own conscience should tell him that certain right wing policies are required at this time.
Anyone with a basic knowledge of economics, and I hope this includes the Minister of Finance, knows that economic recovery can always be hastened by lowering taxes or by using taxation as an incentive rather than a penalty for growth. However, when this logic is put forward by those of us who would like to see job opportunities provided for our young people as well as some of the 625,000 unemployed who are not so young, the Minis-

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada ter of Finance says it would be a dangerous action because it would start another inflationary upsurge and bring about the possible imposition of direct wage and price controls.
There has been so much discussion about inflation during the past few years that we sometimes forget that the fundamental condition for the occurrence of inflation is reasonably full employment of our resources. Prices normally rise when the amount of money that people have to spend increases faster than the supply of goods and services on which they may spend it. This is not the situation today. There is excess production capacity and there is not sufficient consumer demand to purchase all the goods and services that can be placed on the market. It seems logical to everyone but the government that what is needed is more purchasing power in the economy. This is precisely what a tax cut will provide. In my opinion, and in the opinion of Mr. Arthur Smith, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, and other eminent economists, there is absolutely no way in which a tax cut can be generally inflationary in a period of under-employment of resources.
If the government knows of industries or sections within the economy in which there is no excess production capacity, then I believe these industries should be encouraged by tax incentives to locate in areas of regional economic disparity, such as in our northern regions or Atlantic Canada, rather than using the present hit and miss financial handouts as practised by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. Employment opportunities, which are now needed, would then be provide in the north and in the Atlantic provinces where chronic unemployment hovers in some areas at 15 per cent of the work force. Whenever tax cuts are suggested as a means of stimulating the economy to bring it back to full employment, the Minister of Finance takes the position that the government cannot afford the loss of tax revenue which is the end result of a tax cut. This, of course, is nonsense.
The very purpose of a tax cut is to stimulate the economy. It should be obvious to even the present Minister of Finance that at a full employment level the total tax revenue will be considerably greater than when the economy is operating approximately $3 billion below its potential. This is the measure of the gap, as estimated by the Economic Council of Canada, between our actual output at present levels of unemployment and our potential output if unemployment had been approximately 3.8 per cent, and a large source of this untapped potential lies in Canada's north.
In fact, the demographic boundaries of Canada lie in a thin band of population 150 miles wide, running along the American border. Above this area, stretching all the way to the Arctic circle, lies a great band of unused Canadian potential. Typical of government economic thinking, no comprehensive development strategy has been articulated for this vast area. The possible returns to this and future generations are immense yet, thanks to the government's ad hoc approach, the Canadian people are not benefitting from northern development. I believe a comprehensive development strategy for the north would assist the

southern regions of Canada in their economic recovery. With personal incomes down and unemployment up, the Canadian economy desperately needs a shot in the arm. Development of the rich potential of the north would provide this stimulus. This development must be approached systematically. With a forward-looking strategy, Canada's north could be a great contributor to the over-all attainment of Canada's economic potential.
Canadians must seriously ask themselves how many billions of dollars in lost productivity, in wasted resources, both human and material, they can afford before they make a determined effort to get rid of this government. Obviously the government takes the position that during periods of unemployment taxes must be kept high since there are fewer gainfully employed to supply the total revenue needs of the government.
The government and its policies are outdated and my concern is that the errors which have been made to date may be compounded by the introduction of wage and price restraints which could well be the final straitjacket imposed on Canadians by the Liberals. If this is done, I believe the cure would be worse than the disease. Whenever we criticize the government and its suicidal economic policies we are asked: What would you do if you had the responsibility to act? Well, as I have already said, I believe a tax cut is warranted to stimulate the economy. I also believe that inflationary pressure in the south is caused in part by bottlenecks in the economy. In these areas of the south, stress could be relieved by providing business with opportunities to expand, and an excellent way of doing this would be to make provision for greater opportunities in the northern regions.
A large area of Canada has been classified as the "mid-Canada corridor". In my opinion this area, rich in resources but sparsely populated, should provide the first take-off area for development. Obviously, the Regional Development Incentives Act, as administered by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, has not done the job it should have done because its purpose has not been developed in the larger context of a northern development strategy. The mid-Canada corridor is a project which calls for a hard second look by the government. We can afford to start development now. In fact, if our potential is not to be lost forever, we must start development of the north now.
In the Ottawa area some economies could be carried out and I believe the Minister of Finance would do well to consider the appointment of an all-party committee of Members of Parliament interested in finance to act as a kind of financial ombudsman in the examination of projected programs and expenditures. There are a number of sacred cows around Ottawa and in my view it is time some of their horns were clipped. Consider the CBC, for example. I do not advocate selling the corporation but it would be interesting to see what would happen if the management of the CBC were to be informed that a deficit of $2 million a week, or $104 million a year, was the largest amount acceptable to the government instead of the $165 million deficit listed for the CBC this year.
May 11, 1971

Undoubtedly some programs would have to be curtailed, but the $61 million saved could provide a considerable amount of aid to the 165,000 Indian people presently living in Canada.
As I mentioned earlier, the Prices and Incomes Commission and its expensive staff of economists is only window dressing which adds to the load of the taxpayers without solving any of their problems. In my opinion, and in my opinion alone, it should be abolished. In fact, I have grave doubts whether the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs established in 1967 can justify its cost to the Canadian people.
In conclusion, I implore this government to seriously reconsider its present policies relating to the north, as well as to the rest of Canada, in the hope that productivity, incentive and even the normal desire to build or expand a business are given some encouragement and result in the reduction of the numbers unemployed. Both unemployment and inflation vie for position as our number one problem. I do not believe we can effectively deal with the other needs of our society until we have shown ourselves capable of solving these two problems.
