speechtext:
I must say that the tone of doom and gloom with which the previous speaker put his ideas forward reminded me of an old Presbyterian clergyman in the province from which that hon. member comes. Addressing the congregation about their sins, he said: I tell you that you will be up to your necks in boiling brimstone and there will be devils poking pitchforks into you and you will lift your eyes from the smoke and say to the Lord "Laird, Laird, we didna ken." And the Lord in His infinite compassion and mercy will look down on you and He will say "Well, ye ken the noo."
For myself, I intend to deal with only one aspect of this subject, namely, the development of the north and, particularly, the development of oil and gas reserves. I listened with considerable interest to the speech of the leader of the New Democratic Party. I share some of the concern he expressed. I share his concern for the future of the native people as development proceeds, because such development could be damaging. I also share his concern about damage to the environment. We all know this is possible, and if we neglect to take
Development of Northern Canada adequate precautions it becomes probable. What bothers me about the speech of the leader of the NDP, as well as
other speeches which have been made recently is this___
they seem to reflect a counsel of despair.
Because there are risks attached to the development of the north, because there are risks to the environment, because there is the possibility that the native people will not be helped by such development, they seem to argue that the only course to take is to do nothing. They seem to argue that we ought not to seek solutions or attempt to find a secure and positive method of developing the north but, rather, that we should leave the north in cold storage. This is certainly not the way in which we developed the Canadian west and it is not the kind of spirit in which we shall develop the Canadian north, either.
The leader of the New Democratic Party appears to see a considerable distinction between the sale of renewable resources and non-renewable resources. Part of his criticism of northern development appears to be an opposition to the extraction of oil and its sale abroad, specifically to the United States. Apparently in his view there is something wrong with finding oil, taking it out of the ground and selling it. I wish he would explain that to the people of the province of Alberta and of northern British Columbia who have prospered to a very considerable degree from the oil industry.
Admittedly, we cannot export more than our surplus of non-renewable resources, but surely surpluses are for selling. If there is something economically wrong with selling a non-renewable resource, such as oil, gas, coal, nickel and such minerals, does it then follow that it is quite all right to sell renewable resources, such as grain-I suppose the hon. member would agree with this-lumber and pulp which, as long as we do not overcut our forests, are renewable resources? Among renewable resources that could be sold is water. Water is clearly a renewable resource, for as long as the winds blow and deposit rain and our lakes and rivers flow down to the sea, we shall have water. I wonder whether he would favour the sale of water abroad; I doubt very much that he would. I do not think I would myself, even though it is a renewable resource. There is nothing sacred about the words "non-renewable" and "renewable". Decisions must be made in light of current conditions and a reasoned and sensible estimation of what the future may hold.
The hon. member also spoke of the desirability of settlement in the north and the desirability of developing such industries as smelters in the north. Certainly, I could not agree with him more, except that I would point out that in some areas of the north, specifically the Northwest Territories, the sub-Arctic and true Arctic regions, we are faced with conditions that are in many ways very different from those in the south. The suggestion to build a smelter is interesting enough in this regard. Smelters are notorious for the emission of great quantities of pollution into the air from their stacks. I think most hon. members are familiar with the extent to which air pollution is increased by what is called a

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada temperature inversion. When Los Angeles or Montreal has a temperature inversion in the atmosphere lasting for two or three days, the results are quite noticeable and quite serious.
We should take into account that over much of the Northwest Territories in winter a temperature inversion frequently develops and lasts for a month to a month and a half. Therefore, we may find some developments which, though suitable to the south, cannot be established in the north. I hope there are not but it is possible that there are. In any event, I believe it surely cannot be beyond the ingenuity of our technicians in Canada, or even in the world community, to develop safe delivery systems for oil and gas not only out of the northern mainland but out of the high Arctic.
A great many methods of transport are being considered at the moment for the high Arctic. The northern development committee has heard evidence in this respect from a number of witnesses. To review it briefly, if oil is discovered in, say, the Sverdrup group-and gas has already been discovered on King Christian Island in quantities that would constitute a commercial field if discovered in southern Canada-delivery of oil would almost certainly have to take place by undersea pipeline; by the use of Manhattan-type ice-strengthened tankers with icebreaker support; by submarine tankers of 170,000 tons and above operating in open water to Godthab, Greenland, or down to Trinity, Newfoundland, or by what is called a semi-submersible submarine. This is a new idea not yet fully developed which calls for a submarine to operate near the surface with a tall 16-foot steel sail, so-called, cutting through the ice, the ship being capable of submerging and running on a closed circuit, oxygen-breathing diesel system for sufficient time to move underneath the pressure ridges when the barrier of ice is more than can be cut by the sail.
The committee was also informed-and such is the progress of technology that I do not suppose this will surprise members of the House-that it is not inconceivable that delivery of oil out of the high Arctic by air is possible in the foreseeable future. The cost of heavy air transport is down to three and a half cents per ton mile in the United States at the present time. At least one witness before the committee clearly saw the possibility of the cost of air transport coming down to two and a half cents and eventually to one cent per ton mile.
So, if and when a major discovery of oil is made in the high Arctic, and I think most people who have been observing developments up there would say it is a question of when rather than if, we will be faced with the necessity of doing some adventurous engineering and will need some adventurous and very able people in that part of Canada. Hopefully-indeed, we should insist and demand-the people who are most experienced in the high north, namely the Eskimo and further to the south the Indian, should use their very real and practical expertise in the exploratory and development stages. They should be trained as quickly as possible to take over the ever-increasingly technical aspects of the operation. In this respect the more they take over, the better.
However, there is a difficulty we must face both in the employment of these people in the north and in determining how we are going to get the oil out of these islands. We cannot move too far in the preparation of means of transit for oil out of the high Arctic until we have found the oil. Equally, I can see a danger in too hurriedly giving Eskimos and northern Indians specialized training for pipeline work and other technical jobs if we fail to discover oil in the north. It is bad enough that the training of these people for modern society is, with the exception of a few young people, not as advanced as it should be.
We must hope that the people who have to make the decisions are wise enough to chart these two lines so that they cross at the right point. It is important that our Eskimos and northern Indians be given training to take over most of the technical jobs in the north at the time they become available. Their training must begin at a time that will enable them to be ready to take job opportunities that will open for them. If they are not trained in time we face the prospect of southern whites taking these jobs in the absence of a trained labour pool in the north. If their training is given too early, it will be a tremendous and bitter disappointment to them if jobs fail to materialize.
In any event, I do not want to take more time of the House except to repeat a point I made earlier. We should not look upon the north as a parkland we intend to leave unspoiled, because leaving it unspoiled in its natural state will also mean leaving it with a rapidly increasing population of Eskimos and Indians who really do not wish to go back to living in ice houses. They do not want to depend for their living on the Arctic fox. They want what other Canadians want, the right to earn a decent living, to live in homes and decent communities. We cannot accomplish this by sealing Canada at the 60th parallel and leaving an unspoiled wilderness to the Arctic fox.
I favour, and I hope to see, rapid development of the north, within certain limits. There are two severe limits this House and others should be constantly watching. The first is that the rights of native people must be adequately protected. They must be brought into the mainstream of development. The second is that there must be protection for the northern ecology. I thank hon. members for their attention.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ADOPT POLICIES TO DEVELOP THE HUMAN, CAPITAL AND NATURAL RESOURCES OF NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the House who participate in this debate, from whatever approach they take, look to this vast sector of Canada, described by cliche and otherwise, as the undeveloped hinterland of Canada. During this generation we are facing a challenge similar to the one faced by our ancestors 100 years ago during the development of western Canada. I am sure the pioneers 100 years ago looked upon the west with the same degree of hesitation Canadians now experience in respect of the development of the north. They must have looked at weather conditions, the lack of transportation, the lack of
[Mr. St. Pierre.l
May 11, 1971

habitation, the lack of markets for production and sparse population in much the same way we contemplate the north at the present time. The fact is that the west and other parts of Canada which were not developed 100 years ago have now been developed to a tremendous extent, perhaps not as fast as possible, but with considerable success.
Having experienced that development, knowing of the vastly increased number of people and improvements in technology, we as Canadians would be abdicating our responsibility in respect of the development of the rest of the country if we ignored the north. We have in that part of Canada a great number of indigenous people. There is a grave danger that the north will be developed from the white man's point of view. There is a danger that we will be paternalistic in the development of this part of the country without allowing active native participation.
These people have a long way to go in respect of education and technology. They require assistance. There has been a lack and a neglect over the years. It is more than 10 years now since the vision of the north which was derived by many of our opponents as something revolutionary. It was suggested it meant the construction of roads from wigwam to wigwam and from igloo to igloo. There has been a great deal done since that time, and a certain amount is being done now. This effort will have to be increased. It is not and will never be good enough to merely attempt to transplant the Eskimo part way toward the white man's culture. We cannot think in terms of training these people this century and possibly next century up to a certain point, then abandoning them. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) realizes that there is a danger in this regard. We cannot take these people away from their traditional modes of life, give them a smattering of white man's training along with a lot of his bad habits, and then leave them to fend for themselves. We must take a giant step forward in our policies relating to these people of the northland.
Incentives will have to be provided. I doubt if the northland will develop as a result of natural initiatives. I know very little about the eastern Arctic and it is many years since I was in the western Arctic, down the Mackenzie valley. Development was only beginning when I was there 30 years ago. Yellowknife was barely four years old. It was a small hamlet. Today it is the capital of the Northwest Territories. If we wait for natural development we will wait a long time.
We must provide incentives to encourage people from the southern parts of Canada to develop the north. We must convince people in the more populated regions in the south to expand into the north. This is more important than providing the people there with the pill and abortion on demand; that is not the answer and I suggest it is self-defeating. In this part of Canada there exists a tremendous scope for Canadian development. There are tremendous resources yet undiscovered. Incentives must be provided in order to discover and develop these resources and a proper tax system is the way to accomplish this. We need roads, waterways and airways. I do not intend to refer to railroads at the present time, but 24107-11
Development of Northern Canada this kind of development will take place some time in the future. Already we have reached the shores of Great Slave Lake by rail.
In this regard, the present policies of the government are deficient. We have seen the white paper on taxation, but such a policy would quite frankly kill any incentives for the development of the north. We are slowing down this potential development if we pursue our present philosophies with regard to resource development, and the imposition of taxes on the production of primary resources. There cannot be any differentation between that land north of the 60th parallel and the land to the south. We must treat our mining companies, lumber companies and oil companies on the same basis across Canada. We must not adopt attitudes which will destroy incentives to resource development companies and individuals, including unincorporated syndicates who are interested.
In the past, we have given opportunities to foreigners who enjoyed a considerable tax advantage over our own Canadians in the development of our resources. One only has to look at the late forties and early fifties when Canadians who were trying to participate in the development of the oil industry in Alberta and Saskatchewan were beaten to the post every time, particularly by our friends in the United States whose tax laws were much more favourable. Therefore, I say the policies of the government with regard to tax law and tax incentives in respect of resource development have been wrong. If the government persists in the recommendations contained in the white paper it will eternally condemn the north to stagnation, unless that development takes place through public ownership and public participation entirely. This may suit a number of people, but I suggest the history of our performance in that type of development has been indeed a sad and sorry one.
Let us consider transportation. Yes; there are roads. There cannot be an instant system of highways. There has been a certain amount of work in this regard but more could have been done. Then, there are such things as aids to navigation along the Mackenzie. These could be improved. The lack of insistence, for instance, on permits at the time of the construction of the Bennett dam was something that worked against the development of the north because that dam has affected the water levels on the navigable portions of the Mackenzie. In respect of air, last year we saw an ill-fated proposal by the government to tax airline tickets on a percentage basis. If there was ever anything designed to stultify the development of the north it was this proposal. I admit it applies to aircraft of certain size, and that there were exemptions, but the tax applied to passengers going by regular carriers such as Pacific Western Airlines to the down-river posts and the Arctic. What a way to strangle development! Well, somehow or other I think we finally got to the government and it saw how ill-advised this policy was.

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada
Here again, I believe the lack of a real regional air carrier policy will also work to the detriment of the north. I say we must have an inquiry into our domestic air policy. I think the Globe and Mail was quite correct in its editorial yesterday concerning the policy of our national air carriers in respect of domestic flights, and the fact that it is costing Canadians far more than should be the case. For that reason, I say we must have an inquiry in order to determine a far better national air policy for Canadians. This will also affect the north.
In the limited time I have available to me, I want to say Canadians must be encouraged to participate in the development of the north since they have an equity in it. There is no such suggestion in the present plan. Where is it suggested that these developments in the North are to be owned by Canadians? I made these proposals during the hearings of the Finance Committee in respect of tax reform, but I want to make them again. I would be very discriminatory in favour of Canadians and Canadian companies, truly owned by Canadians, in the resource development field, be it mining, be it lumbering or be it exploration and production of oil and gas.
In respect of these things which represent the development of our primary resources, Canadians should enjoy a certain tax advantage. If we were to have a capital gains tax such a person should be exempt in respect of any gains made in that field, provided the investment remained in the resource development sector. He could move around from one mine to another mine or from a mining company to a lumbering company or from a lumbering company to an oil and gas company, but there should be encouragement for him to remain within these fields. If the tax is to be 25 per cent, and if he remained there for one year, he would pay the 25 per cent tax. However, if he remained a second year it would be reduced by 5 per cent and if he remained a third year it would be reduced by 10 per cent, then 15 per cent and so on all the way down. If he remained there five years there would be no capital gains tax. That is a medium range investment, but I would say it is a sufficient encouragement to Canadians to participate in the development of their own resources. It would be an advantage for Canadians. I do not deny there is discrimination against an outsider and you may say, in so far as that taxpayer is concerned, there is discrimination in favour of him as against an investor in a manufacturing company in central Canada. Yes, there is, but I have a stated objective.
The objective is greater ownership and participation by Canadians in the development of their own resources. It is not by setting up Crown corporations that you will guarantee this. It will not be done by setting up a Canadian Development Corporation, as we now see it and are studying it in the Finance Committee. This Corporation will be a non-starter in so far as this type of development is concerned. It will not accomplish the purpose. We want Canadians from one end of our country to the other to be able to participate in the development of the resources of our vast north. Certainly there are many safeguards involved.

Members will speak about ecology and so on, but it is still possible to carry out this development of resources which will bring people to the north and see to the development of the north. If one said we would require an instant development of the west our ancestors a hundred years ago would have said, "Why, man, you are crazy". But it went step by step. We require transportation and development of our resources to attract people and provide for the economic development of the whole region. However, I do not see much prospect of that happening with the government's present policy. As a matter of fact, I see the reverse. I see an attitude of complete neglect. Some things are being done, but I want to see greater emphasis on this aspect. I want to see emphasis that is applicable in the tax field, with greater assistance through our financial institutions for this type of work. The challenge is there.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks I intend to make will be a change of pace from those of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I intend to confine my remarks to a discussion of one aspect of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), namely, the lack of recognition of the basic and prior rights of the native inhabitants of the territories, including settlement of their claims which would recognize their rights in the land and its resources; because, Mr. Speaker, if there is
May 11, 1971

one single matter about which I have ever-increasing concern as a Canadian, it is the blatant refusal of the government headed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to recognize that aboriginal rights do in fact exist. I must say that this came as a bit of a shock to me in view of the fact that it did appear over a period of several years that the government was moving toward a recognition of aboriginal rights and a willingness to deal in a more realistic way with treaty rights than they had been dealt with in the past.
Hon. members may recall that we had two versions of a bid on this general subject matter introduced in the House, although neither one was fully dealt with. The present Prime Minister, before he became a member of this House, before he became Minister of Justice and later Pr.me Minister, from all the reports I heard of him had been a champion of civil rights and liberties. It is therefore with considerable astonishment and certainly with great regret that I feel the position he has taken, and taken quite adamantly, on the rights of the Indian people is a complete negation of recognition of some of the basic principles of civil liberties and human rights.
_ I think it is time that more and more members of this House came to grips with a determination of this basic question, with particular reference to the north. If we do not, before too long if the present pace of exploration for possible exploitation of the natural resources, particularly the non-renewable resources, continues the problem in that area of the country, as has been the case in the past m other parts of the country, will be so late being dealt with that it will be too late for it to be dealt with meaningfully.
The time has come when members of the House should begin to turn their attention to the booklet which was published as the result of a research study by the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada, entitled "Native Rights in Canada." I intend to devote at least part of the time that I have today to putting into the records of this House some of the things which are said in this book The introduction reads:
The issues around Canada's aboriginal peoples are, even today, not separable from Canada's particular history of Indian-tvhite relations. To look at the present we must understand the pas . The emergence of a newer Indian leadership does not change this fact. The new organizations and the new leaders are at least as concerned with the issues of treaty and aboriginal rights as their predecessors.
I think that is a true statement. I had the pleasure and honour of knowing, to some extent at least, the great, late Reverend Dr. Peter Kelly, a chieftain of the Haida,' one of the pioneer leaders of the Indian people who first appeared and made their voices heard before members of this House. His concern for and knowledge of the whole question were deep.
But I think it is true to say, as the introduction to this publication points out, that the new leaders of the Indian peoples have as deep a concern as did people like the late Reverend Dr. Peter Kelly who, as some hon. members may know, in addition to being a chief of the Haida was an ordained minister of the United Church of Canada who was chosen by his church to head the British 24107-11|
Development of Northern Canada Columbia conference some years before his death. The phrase, "To look at the present we must understand the past," I think is the key point in that quotation.
That, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, apparently is exactly what the Prime Minister does not understand or refuses to recognize. In fact, I would say that the only way one can describe him in this context is to label him an historical illiterate, which seems rather surprising if one looks at the record of his academic achievement and his fields of interest as set forth in the Parliamentary Guide. In it we read that he studied law at the University of Montreal, graduating with honours, and undertook postgraduate studies in law, economics and political science in Paris and at the London School of Economics. When he was in practice he specialized in labour law and civil liberties cases in Quebec, and became associate Professor of law at the University of Montreal where he taught constitutional law, civil liberties and carried out research.
All I can say is that during that period of his career the Prime Minister could not have conducted any research into the question of the basic concepts of civil liberties as they apply to the Indian people of Canada.
There is no record of that kind after my name in the Parliamentary Guide, although I was an honours student in history at the University of British Columbia. I do not make the charge of historical illiteracy against the Prime Minister only on my own knowledge, but after reading with interest and I hope some degree of understanding the contents of this book.
This is not a haphazard publication but is the result of a research grant from a foundation in Calgary. The head of the research committee was Dean R. J. Macdonald of the faculty of law, University of Toronto. Mr. Alfred Best, Q.C., Mr. T. A. King, Q.C., Mr. Malcolm Montgomery, Mr. T. H. B. Symons, Mr. B. J. MacKinnon, Q.C., and Mr. I. Binnie were members of the committee. Director of the research staff was Douglas Sanders, faculty of law, University of Windsor. Research associates were Kenneth Lysyk, faculty of law, University of British Columbia, and Anthony Hooper, faculty of law, Laval University.
Having read the book, I feel that I am not alone in my appraisal of the position taken by the Prime Minister in turning his back on the question of aboriginal rights. In an appendix there are quotations from a speech made by the Prime Minister on August 8, 1969, in Vancouver on the subject of Indian aboriginal and treaty rights. He refers to the fact that the government had come up with a proposal, a policy paper on the Indian problem which proposed a set of solutions. "It doesn't impose them on anybody", said the Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, some of these things were imposed upon the Indian people long before the white paper policy was presented to this House. It is all very well for the Prime Minister to say that this white paper does not impose anything on the Indian people, but I suggest that it does not propose- -it rejects the alleviation of some of the things already imposed upon the Indian people. If we are to understand

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada the present we must have some understanding of the past.
The Prime Minister went on to talk about some of the choices before Canadians generally and before the Indian peoples within our boundaries in particular. He said the question was the following:
-whether Canadians as a whole want to continue treating the Indian populations as something outside, a group of Canadians with which we have treaties, a group of Canadians who have as the Indians, many of them claim, aboriginal rights or whether we will say well forget the past and begin today and this is a tremendously difficult choice because, if-well one of the things the Indian bands often refer to are their aboriginal rights and in our policy, the way we propose it, we say we won't recognize aboriginal rights. We will recognize treaty rights. We will recognize forms of contract which have been made with the Indian people by the Crown and we will try to bring justice in that area and this will mean that perhaps the treaties shouldn't go on forever.
He went on to talk about its being inconceivable to have treaties between peoples within a single nation, as if the treaties and all they stand for were only concerned with whether the Indians were to receive a little twine and gunpowder. This strikes me as approaching the whole question of treaties with sneering contempt, without any appreciation of historical significance. This is something that is separate and apart from the matter of aboriginal rights. Later he said:
But aboriginal rights, this really means saying, "We were here before you. You came and you took the land from us and perhaps you cheated us by giving us some worthless things in return for vast expanses of land and we want to reopen this question. We want you to preserve our aboriginal rights and to restore them to us." And our answer-it may not be the right one and may not be one which is accepted but it will be up to all of you people to make your minds up and to choose for or against it and to discuss with the Indians-our answer is no .
He went on to refer to a statement of the late President Kennedy regarding the question of the Negro people in American society and quoted with approbation, We will be just in our time. This is all we can do. We must be just today." I agree with the sentiment expressed by the late President Kennedy as strongly as does the Prime Minister. What I am suggesting is that the Prime Minister either cannot or will not see what is involved here. When he interprets the Indians' plea as, "We want you to preserve our aboriginal rights and to restore them to us, this is not my understanding of what they have been trying to tell us.
They recognize that we cannot turn back the clock. None of my Indian friends has ever told me that they want the white man to go back across the seas where he came from, and not return. They recognize that we are here and that they are a minority. They are not asking us to do as some of the colonial powers have in territories in Africa and Asia where the white people have always been in the minority. They are only asking us to recognize their aboriginal rights, to sit down and negotiate a settlement of them. "Then, and then only, they say "we can become part of the same society with the rest of you. Then, and then only, can we discuss whether the ancient treaties should continue."

It is my submission that if we are prepared to accept the reality of aboriginal rights, the suggestion of the Prime Minister that the treaties should not necessarily continue is something that the Indian people would be willing to discuss. Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I have lost track of how much time I have left. If I have a few minutes more I would make one or two further references to this book. On page 14 it deals with the origin of the concept of aboriginal titles. I commend this book to hon. members. The book points out that this concept goes back a long way in history, that it is basic to the notion of native rights, that it is not a matter which has been thoroughly studied in this day and age-actually, this little volume is a pioneering work in this field-that it developed really with the beginning of the occupation of North America by people from Europe, and that one of the earliest nations to be concerned about this question and come to grips with it was Spain. It reads on page 14:

Charles V sought the advice of the foremost theologian of the day, Franciscus de Vittoria, a humanist and a friend of Erasmus. Vittoria was Professor of Sacred Theology at the University of Salamanca. He gave two lectures in 1532, which are recorded in his book ... in which he deals with basic questions of Indian rights and the question of slavery. Vittoria asserted that the Indians were the true owners of the land both from the public and the private point of view. Their lack of belief in the Roman Catholic faith could not affect the question, as heretics in Europe were not denied property rights. He suggested that the Indians were no less intelligent than some Spanish peasants and therefore were equally fit to have legal rights.
The author goes on to suggest that the Spanish had the right to travel into Indian lands so long as they did no harm to the natives, for, says the author, "hospitality is part of the law of nations". Also, the Spanish had the right to trade with the Indians. In certain circumstances, if the Indians were to deny these rights after reasonable explanation, the Spanish could lawfully make war. Otherwise, the Spanish could not wage a just war and by that means claim rights by conquest. In 1537 Pope Paul III used the Bull Sublimus Deus and the author quotes from it as follows:
-Indians are truly men ... they may and should freely and legitimately enjoy their liberty and the possession of their property nor should they be in any way enslaved; should the contrary happen, it .shall be null and of no effect.

Before the dinner hour, Mr. Speaker, I had mentioned that the motion very generously presumes that the government has policies. It is a fallacious presumption but nevertheless it is the gist of the motion. My remarks were directed toward the fact that neither this nor any previous government has really had time to formulate policies. We work from one moment to the next and one panic to another. We had no policy on the export of energy resources until Denison Mines was going to be sold; then suddenly we made a decision. Then there was the situation with regard to Home Oil. The shirt and textile manufacturers got after the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and he immediately had a policy for that.
What the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) objected to was that under our parliamentary system it is almost impossible to form policies for any length of time. In order to remedy this system it is not enough to just make remarks about it. The whole system must be changed to a great extent. That may mean the introduction of certain republican ideas or congressional ideas, or a mixture of the two merged with the parliamentary system. It just will not work the present way, nor can we expect the government to have policies for any length of time.
This motion concerns northern development. If I heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) correctly, his idea of development means immediate exploitation. His idea of development seems to be to get the resources out of the ground, sell them quickly and get rid of our energy, including hydroelectric power in the north, because there is reason to get rid of them very quickly. If we examine this situation carefully, we will see that usually the corporation or exploitation company is controlled by an American company which desires to develop the resources to sell to Americans. They want to beat other American companies who are importing from various parts of the world, at the same time leaving a tiny residue of resources in respect of which Canadians can build pipelines, as has been stated by the minister.
I visited these areas and talked with some of the people who are working on the projects. The presumption, of course, is that a great many qualified Canadian will have jobs in perpetuity. But oil riggers are, by and large, members of an international pool and their headquarters are in Dallas, Texas. The pipe manufacturers-

For example, it is not enough to say to the Americans, "You can have $6 billion worth of gas provided we have some labour content." It is time for us to say, rather, "You can have $6 billion worth of gas, but this represents energy you do not possess and that energy will produce for you Americans $50 billion worth of employment. Therefore, if we can reach some agreement by which Canadians will be ensured of $25 billion worth of employment, you can have the gas." The same line of thought can be applied in the case of hydroelectric exports. But we are still working on outdated assumptions and at no time have we stopped to formulate such policies, because we are apprehensive that a small segment of our society will complain on the ground that the resources are there and we are not getting rid of them.
Most of us are cognizant of the problem involved here, particularly as it concerns the export of our gas and the transportation of Alaska oil. I think evey hon. member should read carefully the proceedings of the Special Committee on Environment and Pollution, issue No. 17. The witnesses before the committee were Dr. Fuller, Dr. Lambert and Mr. Passmore, members of a special task force examining the pipeline question and the proposed route by tanker.
It is important to note-the evidence they gave bears this out-that at the present time the government should be in no hurry to allow the export of gas nor, indeed, the construction of a pipeline through the Mackenzie Valley. The witnesses whose names I have mentioned pointed out that the pipeline, if built, would pass through two earthquake zones. Moreover, no one can tell what the ecological consequences of an oil spill might be, since sufficient research work has not been done. I believe it is now acknowledged that there will be a spill, whether a tanker spill or a pipeline spill, and until more research has been carried out it is not possible to predict the results.
The scientists also pointed out to the committee that insufficient attention had been paid to the possibility of using other transportation systems such as the Alaska Highway or railroad system along conventional lines, or a monorail system. We are going pell-mell into a situation in circumstances in which we are not obliged to do so. We think we have to do these things. We think it is essential to get this oil to the United States because ten years from now it may not be of any use.
The fact is that ten years from now the petrochemical industry may be willing to pay a lot more for these resources. Why this great rush, until we have investigated? The evidence is that it would take a minimum of five years before we could know what the consequences may be. The real question, therefore, is how we could prevent
the Americans risking an oil spill. After all, it is their oil in Alaska.
I believe the government should realize that we are sitting in Canada with a powerful hand. We need not send out battleships, soldiers or anything like that. But we need to say firmly that we have a policy, or propose to have a policy, based on research, on an accurate estimate of the reserves which will be needed by ourselves and others, tied to benefits to our own productive capacity. Then we should say to the Americans, "If you really insist, you can take your oil by tanker from Valdez to a point near Seattle, but we shall not like it. You happen to need our water to keep your Imperial Valley growing vegetables; you also require our uranium, our nickel and our ore. If you displease us, remember we control these resources."
I think it will need no more than that because, after all, the Americans are well aware of our position and some of them are not too keen about rushing headlong into the type of oil transportation which, of course, some of the companies desire. If the government of the United States realized we had a policy and were adamant on it, I am sure we would get co-operation.
It comes down to this. Canadians elected a government which we expect would be courageous, daring and inventive. But somehow all these clouded policy issues have convinced our people that we as a government are not daring, but cautious; that we are not inventive, but that we cling to conventional ways of thinking. This is what influences our lives. The capital is here. If we want it, we have it. We can do all these things. I think the government should pay attention to this disenchantment and ask, "Why are we here?" The answer should be, "we are here because we have been elected to do these great things, and we can do them." Therefore, I believe the second part of the motion has a great deal of substance.

Mr. Speaker, the House is asked to consider a most important question, and I believe that the official opposition was justified in

May 11, 1971

proposing the non-confidence motion appearing on the Order Paper so that this government would state which measures it proposes to take in the shortest possible order to rationalize the development of our natural resources to enable Canadians to exploit them as fully as possible.
Last fall, I visited the North with a House committee and I was enthralled by the magnitude of its untapped natural resources, while in Canada there are today thousands of unemployed who would be only too happy to see the government implement a rational planning policy to launch the development of these resources for the benefit of the nation as a whole.
It is difficult, in a debate such as this, as a member from Quebec, not to say a word about the James Bay project. We know that immediately after the announcement of this project by the premier of Quebec, authorities involved in the fields of politics, sociology and economics expressed their views.
This project, Mr. Speaker, will cost almost $6 billion. Three rivers will be used: the Nottaway, Broadback and Rupert rivers. There is a possibility to extend this number to five. Here, I make a digression to point out that this is where the federal government plays its part. If we follow the policies of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), who urged the provinces not to borrow too much on the foreign market, the minister will have to take his responsibilities and tell Quebec how to negotiate its loans on the Canadian market. Mr. Speaker, the keen observer sees at a glance the vastness of the project not only for Quebec but for the rest of Canada also.
Quebec has furnished evidence of its efficiency in this field: let us consider the Manicouagan and Outardes projects for instance. One passes rapidly from great amazement to questions which remain unanswered. As a French-Canadian member of the House, I have a right to doubt the profit-earning capacity of such a project.
Will this project encourage the development of northern Quebec? Will the electric power produced be used in developing industry in this region? Unfortunately, up until now nothing points to such an accomplishment. Besides water which resources can we draw from this region? The forests are sufficiently exploited and we have no more need for gold.
If my hon. friend who just interrupted me would read today's La Presse, he would notice that this project is

Will other resources be processed in the United States, in Quebec or somewhere else in Canada? After its $6 billion investment in that hydro-electric project will Quebec have the capital needed to develop and process these resources?

Mr. Speaker, I intend to confine my remarks this evening to two main areas which are the responsibility of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). The initial area which I should like to discuss relates to one aspect of the social policies of this government. I believe it is an aspect which has frequently been criticized in the past, but from my personal experience in visiting a number of Indian communities it is evident that we have made enormous progress over the last few years in providing adequate and improved housing for our Indian and Eskimo people. The Indian and Eskimo housing program has already resulted in more than 11,000 new homes having been built. This year alone more than 2,000 homes will be added to the 11,000 total. Without question, we are improving the strictly material aspects of our social policy vis-a-vis the Indian and Eskimo people of Canada.
I am afraid the record is less satisfactory when we look at some of the results of our social policy in the educational and employment field, although I realize that there too the government is making enormous strides. Important new programs have been developed over the past three or four years and these are beginning to produce results. However, I do not think anyone in this government is satisfied with the present unemployment rate among our Indian people, nor is anyone in the government satisfied with the extremely high drop-out rate of Indian youngsters, particularly in our high schools. This drop-out rate is close to four times the national average and unemployment rate ranges, at least for part of the year, between 40 per cent and 50 per cent.
Having said that, I do not think there is any hesitation on the part of this government to take whatever action is necessary and to inaugurate whatever new policy may be necessary to reduce the rates of unemployment and

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada drop-outs among our Indian students, rates which belie the material progress the government has been making in providing for the physical wants of our indigenous peoples. '
Clearly, the most important thing this government has accomplished in the last few years is the provision of the mechanisms by which our Indian people can act on their own and can take the initiative in solving their own problems. Increasingly in the last several years we have seen Indian organizations spring up, representing every provincial group of Indians. A strong national organization has also been developed. These organizations are not yes-men for any government. They are making gains on behalf of the Indian people they represent in a very forceful and effective way.
This is producing results for the Indian people and is instilling pride in them when they are able to see the results of the new forcefulness translated into government action. The mechanisms which have been provided to allow our Indian and Eskimo people to take this selfinitiative will in the long run, I believe, prove to have been the most important thing we have done in this transitional period which started in the late 1950s, really, and accelerated during the early 1960s-a period in which we have seen the number of Indian and Eskimo children in high school multiply many times over, and the number of children in university increase many fold.

I should like to deal particularly with one area of the north, northern Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Quebec government will have to hurry its consideration of Indian claims to prevent its James Bay project from being hampered by legal proceedings.
I believe that the Quebec government's position when dealing with the Indian people, in particular those living in the so-called New Quebec area, is untenable. No doubt people know that when the federal government in 1912 transferred jurisdiction on the New Quebec territory to the Quebec government, the latter assumed responsibility for direct settlement of all the claims the Indians in the area could make. Up to now, those claims have never been sustained and, if the Quebec government does not want to see its James Bay project obstructed indefinitely, it is most important that the native rights issue in the New Quebec area be settled.
The other area I would like to touch upon tonight concerns the resource policy of the government as it relates to the oil and gas regulations which have been

under suspension for some time now. I do not remember precisely when the suspension first took effect, but it seems to me it is more than a year ago since the oil and gas regulations applicable to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon were suspended.
Up until they were suspended the basic philosophy behind the regulations was that the permit holder should have first choice of 50 per cent of his permit area and that should return the remainder to the Crown. The choices were subject to certain restrictions, but in any event they all boiled down to a 50 per cent turnback to the Crown in the event of a discovery of normal size. There were a whole series of explanatory rules which provided for the discovered resources to be separated one from another by a row of sections, or that the permit holder could choose his section squares on an alternate basis; but the end result was that the Crown kept its 50 per cent.
The practice in the provinces has been for this 50 per cent to be auctioned off to the highest bidder. The regulations were different in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon, at least until they were suspended. They provided that the Crown's 50 per cent was subject to the original permit holder's option to take it, as well, by paying a double royalty. This was an additional incentive, and it was judged to be necessary to encourage the higher risk and cost of exploration in the Northwest Territories. It had that effect; it did encourage a certain amount of risk capital that would not have gone there had this additional incentive not existed. But at the time when the discoveries were made at Prudhoe Bay, all this changed and in this changed situation there was no longer any requirement on the part of the Crown, in my view, to provide this additional incentive.
The potential which was demonstrated by the Prudhoe Bay discoveries, the potential which the Arctic area held for possible oil and gas discoveries was such that this double royalty clause was no longer a justified sweetener for the purposes of getting additional risk capital into exploration.
What concerns me now is the likely direction in which I feel the regultions may be changed. It is reasonable to expect that there will be a tendency on the part of the government to opt for the type of option regulations which already exist in the provinces and which have proven effective in a province like Alberta. These option regulations have given Alberta a fairly high percentage return on its oil resources, when all taxes, federal and provincial, and the royalities are taken into consideration. If Alberta is compared with oil producing countries throughout the world, then the results there compare fairly well. But the Alberta regulations have resulted in a situation which I think most of us deplore, in that the percentage of foreign control of the oil and gas resources in Alberta, and throughout the Canadian west, ranges well over 85 per cent.
This has been a result of this policy and I would like to suggest to the government, as I did in a previous speech- if I remember correctly, last June-that instead of the 50 per cent that is returned to the Crown being auctioned-
May 11, 1971

off, it be retained by the Crown or at least remain directly under Crown control or ownership, possibly with farm-out provisions, perhaps with first preference going to the original permit holder.

Development of Northern Canada
Up to 1J years ago the people of Goose Bay, one of the other two populated areas in Labrador, depended 100 per cent upon the activities of the United States Air Force base. In the last year or so there has been a wood exporting operation that sort of comes and goes and seems to operate on no firm basis. Generally speaking, the economy of the area still depends for all practical purposes solely upon the operation of the base.
As was done in connection with the other, similar United States installations in Newfoundland, we have been given indications that despite assurances to the contrary there is a possibility that this base might fold. Recently a small curtailment of the activities of the base was announced, causing the people of the area great concern. Between 8,000 and 9,000 people depend solely on this base. I am asking, relative to the motion: What action is being contemplated by the government, which has a responsibility in this area, in the event that the base should close? What will it do after consulting the province? Except for a few desultory or token signs of activity, there is no sign of proposed action.
Let me say that when the base at St. John's, Newfoundland, closed the population affected was absorbed by the larger population of the town. There is no large population in Goose Bay which could absorb the people affected by the closure of the base. I have read that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is interested in making deals with provincial governments and setting up what they call infrastructure. Infrastructure, as I understand it, is a variety of amenities that may improve the economic and social climate. It may entice or encourage industry to come into the area.
There is no sign of any infrastructure program being undertaken in Goose Bay. There is no program, apart from plans with federal participation to build a vocational training school-I do not know what good that will do-for creating an economic climate that will induce industry to the area. As I say, I do not know what good that will do or I do not know what I am talking about. I presume that the people who live in such northern communities could move to the pollution-ridden areas of the south.
I remember vividly one night this past winter boarding an aircraft to fly to Newfoundland. It was a murky evening in Ottawa, with a low cloud ceiling, the kind of ceiling that helps you to appreciate fully the odour that comes from the factory across the river. That night I could hardly breathe. At midnight I left for Goose Bay and a few hours later, five or six to be exact, I landed in Goose Bay on a frosty, clear morning. It was wonderful to get off the aircraft and breathe pure, fresh air. It smelled fresh. One cannot describe it except by saying that it smelled like pure, fresh air.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the motion now before us is of the utmost importance since it will enable Parliament to consider the possibilities of developing our natural resources in the Canadian North.
When in school, I remember having the map of Canada explained to me over and over again I was always so fascinated by the teacher's explanations. Some years ago we could read on top of the map the words-"Dominion of Canada."

May 11, 1971
Development of Northern Canada
e (9:30 p.m.)
A few years later, the name was "Dominion of Canada" while the north changed neither in location nor in name. It was still the north, still the Arctic, still an immense territory which we were told was peopled with Eskimos and Indians, an immense tract of land unfit for white men's settlement, covered by ice and devoid of any resources men could benefit by.
Now, after reading the motion brought forward, I went out of my way to study the history of that vast territory in order to find out how it has been administered in past years, the past 90 or 100 years, and that is when I really understood why the motion has been brought before the House.
The motion is worded as follows:
That this House believes that an enlightened program of human and economic progress for Northern Canada offers great opportunities for the people of this country; and that the economic and social policies of the present government have brought about confusion and delayed progress; and that it is essential to make appropriate changes in our approach in respect of Northern Canada;
It is advisable, I believe, to take a quick look at what happened in the past and at the form of government that existed in the Northern Territories. The Act of 1869 concerning the transitional government provided for the first time for the administration of the land of Rupert and the Northwest Territories. But this legislaion was replaced by the Act of 1870.
Following the creation of Saskatchewan and Alberta the Northwest Territories government saw its status reduced to that which existed before 1870. The Act of 1905 established a council of four members appointed by the government, but no appointment was made during 16 years. An appointment was expected but none was made. After 16 years, a commissioner was appointed and given all powers that had been so far those of the Lieutenant Governor, the Executive Council and the Assembly of the Northern Territories. One man was carrying out all these duties.
The first commissioner was Colonel White, a Northern Mounted Police controller, who, from Ottawa, administered the territories, while carrying out his other duties. It is not surprising then that the North was developed very slowly, as it was administered almost in the same way as it had always been since the time of the fur trade.
It is in 1963 only that the duties of the Commissioner of the North were separated from those of the deputy minister of the federal department in charge of the administration of the northern regions. No territorial law was adopted between 1905 and 1920 and most of the orders made applied to conditions in the Prairies rather than in the region north of the sixtieth parallel.
The present act on the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development gives to the head of this department vast powers for the development of the northern territories, provided he gets the funds required to carry out the projects that are planned.
The present act gives him the non-allocated powers in all matters of federal jurisdiction in the North. The

minister must co-ordinate in the northern territories the activities of the various federal agencies and provide and apply all measures required to ensure a greater economic expansion of the northern territories. He is entrusted with the control and management of all the vacant lands which form the major part of this vast territory. The federal government's interest and authority with regard to Northern development is mainly explained by the Act itself and the department established under the Act.
In general, the federal government is concerned with the Indians and Eskimos living in the Northern Territories where they make up a considerable portion of the population-nearly 60 %- as well as with the development of most of these areas.
The territorial government has no separate and public body to provide the services which are usually available in the provinces, except for the Liquor Board. Employees of the Northern Development department carry out most of the administrative work, they teach school and provide social assistance as well as engineering work.
Since the headquarters of the territorial government is actually in Ottawa and that the commissioner and council members only visit the North occasionally, the average citizen of the northern territories cannot fully appreciate the contribution, which is still very limited, of the territorial government.
The sources of income within the jurisdiction of the territorial government are very limited. Consequently, a very rapid development of this territory is not to be expected unless the central government is willing to make its fiscal policy more beneficial to this territory.
When we read the history of the Canadian territories, we understand better why this region which contains all kinds of resources has not been developed more quickly.
The second part of the motion condemns the government for its failure to promote a truly Canadian strategy for the North based on human, capital and natural resources, and urges that appropriate policies be adopted at once that will bring about such development in that region.
The word "economy", derived from the Greek, means: good use of home resources. If we apply this definition at the national level, it is to be noticed that the word "economics" means good management of public affairs.
According to a division generally accepted, even by economists, three factors are necessary in order to provide men with the goods they need to provide for their wants: nature, work and capital. Those three factors are also necessary when the development of a given territory is concerned.
Sometimes, nature offers some resistance to man. This element is absolutely essential to the production and development of some resources, because without it human activity would be performed in a vacuum and it would be necessary to create, that is to make something out of nothing.
Whether intellectual or manual labour is concerned, it is the only reality which can be described as an active
May 11, 1971

element. Alone it can take some steps in the production and development process of our resources.
Capital is a passive element. It does not exist per se. It is derived from nature and work and is at times fully created by those who have the privilege of controlling the nation's credit.
Nature provides man with a place to dwell, to build shelters, to cultivate the soil, to harvest fruit and vegetables and to breed stocks answering his two most essential needs: food and clothing. Lastly, the subsoil provides industry with minerals and energy.
Since those three components are required in a national economy looking after the needs of its members, it is normal that society, through the organization it has provided for itself and must improve upon, should ensure conservation and control of those three components, if it wants the natural resources-whether located in the Canadian north or elsewhere-to be at the service and fill the human needs of its members, the work to be geared to the fulfilment of the needs of all-not of a few or of some privileged classes-and the instrumental component, that is capital, to serve the appropriate ends of the national economy.
We have in Canada the potential required for the Canadian government to provide for the development of the northern territory. We have there natural resources a great number of which yet to be discovered. We have engineers, tradesmen of all kinds, the most up-to-date machinery in the world which is gathering rust in manufacturers' lots.
In brief, we have everything we need to develop this vast territory, which would provide employment for thousands of young people and make Canada benefit from their abilities. They would be only too happy, once their education completed or even during the summer holidays, to help through their ability and work, people older than they are to develop Canada and to discover throughout its immense territory, in the north or elsewhere, those great resources with which the Providence has endowed our land.
In that area as in others, in order to use human labour and machinery, one must have the necessary finances. In brief, the "dollar" must be available also, which is not the case yet.
Unfortunately, it happens sometimes that without thinking too much about it we believe that the sensibility of those living in northern territories is different from ours.
But after you have met some of them and have discussed with them and when you know their customs and how they want to improve their situation, you realize how much they expect from the Canadian authorities and from the Canadian people to develop all the resources which will enable them to live decently in spite of their primitive customs.
I do not question the goodwill of the minister in charge of this territory but he does not have all the tools required to improve the plight of those northern people.
Development of Northern Canada
Let us grant him the funds required to develop Northern Canada and we shall find that there will be no lack of projects. I am convinced that his staff are finding new projects daily. They are in a position to submit to him the projects which would make it possible to improve the situation, and develop those territories but the minister must often tell them: I should like very much to comply with your wishes, but available funds are limited.
If it were a war project, money would be there at the right time, as we saw in the past, unfortunately, and in adequate amounts. But as it is a peace, project money is not readily available. In fact, there is none. It does not exist in sufficient amounts to implement projects which should normally be implemented during the seventies at the latest because they were not implemented before. This is too bad. It is a logical conclusion in my opinion.
I urge the government to use its majority to subdue our financial system so that it may become a perfect servant for years to come and enable Canadians to build a beautiful country that will belong to them and not to foreigners.
Mr. Speaker, those were the points that I wished to bring to the attention of the House during the debate on this very important motion concerning northern territories. I am convinced that these two days of study on this subject will cause the government to take it into serious consideration and to bring suggestions that will help improve the situation and develop these territories.

Mr. Speaker, development in the north has been a dream shared by millions of Canadians for many years. It was not till the period from 1957 to 1962, a period in which we had a Conservative government, that a genuine and vigorous effort was made to carry out or initiate such development. It was the continued destructive criticism levelled by the Liberal opposition of the day, just as is the case with Liberal members opposite today, which again arrested the development plan just as it was getting under way.
In considering such development every effort must be made to conserve the ecology of the region and to prevent pollution of the air and the water. The best possible living conditions must be offered white and native alike who live there now and who will be going to the north in the future. None of this can be achieved without an over-all, well prepared development policy that is based on research, study, adequate negotiations and consultation with the local residents, and a good deal of effort.
I must stress that orderly development can be achieved only with a nationwide policy of development that is acceptable to the population at large, and in this respect I think there has been a gross failure on the part of the present government. Since the Liberals returned to power in 1963 I think it is fair to say that northern development in all its aspects has been arrested.

speechtext:
If I may return to my remarks, I was saying that Crown corporations such as NCPC have proved in some areas to be obstructive to the orderly development of private enterprise, which on many occasions has proven to be much more efficient than civil service-operated corporations.
New legislation before us such as the Yukon minerals act pose greater possibilities of a slowdown of industrial development, particularly in mining. The possibility of slowdown is getting greater as the days go by. I am pleased to note that the discovery of oil was made before some of the new proposals of this government had been put into effect. I am sure they will cut down the amount of exploration going on in the north.

The slowdown possibilities posed by the Yukon minerals act are typical of this government's economic ability. There is not a comprehensive policy or strategy for this vast area of our country. We have seen nothing but an ad hoc approach and the Canadian people, particularly those of the north, are not benefiting from the kind of northern development that is possible and should be in motion at the present time.
In human and natural resources Canada is probably the world's richest country. Under the feeble guidance of the government this potential lies idle and useless. The Economic Council of Canada has estimated that Canada has lost $3 billion a year in income and jobs because of the economic ineptitude of this government. I think it is fair to say that with the present high rate of unemployment, the sagging economy and the decrease in personal income, the Canadian economy desperately needs a stimulus. The Liberal government has failed to come to grips with this need. The most obvious answer lies in the development of the rich potential of the north.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion has made a feeble effort in what is known as the mid-Canada corridor, with its high resource potential and its sparse population. The approach used has not been in the context of an over-all development strategy, and for this reason alone this government should be served with an eviction notice at the next election.
For many years the Progressive Conservative Party has been a leader in the discussion of how best to utilize our northern resources. We must rekindle this spirit and vigorously press this slothful government for immediate and significant action. As I have mentioned, unemployment at the present time is worse than at anytime since the depression days of the 1930s, but we continue to export our raw resources and by that method we export thousands upon thousands of jobs to other nations. Why are we not developing resources here in Canada? Why are these raw materials not being processed right here? We have the know-how, the manpower and the money to do it. We have a good credit rating if we need more money. What is required is simply a government with development policies. We do not have that.
In considering northern development we must recognize that Canada has need of nationwide purpose. Canada needs a common objective behind which our citizens can gather to contribute individual talents and energies. We are in a position of being able to learn from others' mistakes in the past and avoid repeating them.
At the moment the majority of our population occupies a narrow strip along our southern border and the rest of the country is a tremendous, undeveloped area. We must avoid exploitation and a degradation of Canadian natives. We must avoid uncontrolled pollution of air, water and land. We must avoid indiscriminate destruction of what is in effect the only remaining, virtually untouched, habitable region left on this continent.
We have a unique opportunity. We know there is a need in the world for our natural resources and we should strive to develop them ourselves. We should develop them in a positive way, to the greatest benefit of
May 11, 1971

our citizens. Perhaps it is time to reconsider and rethink the old ideas that our country's greatness depends upon exploitation and export of our raw, natural resources, particularly by high-subsidized corporations which some people consider virtually steal these resources from us to use in their own manufacturing processes, creating jobs in their own country and selling back the finished products at a very handsome profit. This seems to be the basis of the present government's policy. I say it is an outdated policy.
I do not want to be misinterpreted. I should not like anybody to think I am saying we do not need foreign capital. I do want hon. members to think I am saying the government has a responsibility to create an economic climate and mechanisms which would allow Canadians to do more of the developing and have the opportunity to play a greater role in solving unemployment problems and improving the economic despair which has been hanging over us since this government's policies have had the opportunity of becoming effective.
Any program to develop the north must take into account mid-Canada and the Arctic as distinct geographic belts. Development strategy should relate roughly to three distinct parts. There should be a separate program for the development of mid-Canada, there should be a separate program for the development of the Arctic, and there should be an over-all, co-ordinating program whose principal function would be to provide the various support facilities necessary for the implementation of development strategies for mid-Canada and the Arctic region.
Under such a program the rights of the indigenous people must be protected. This matter has been raised on many occasions in the House of Commons. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) have indicated that the native people along the Mackenzie Valley have been consulted with regard to the proposed Mackenzie Valley pipeline construction. Information given to me by the residents of the area would indicate that no such consultations have been held. I notice the minister looking in the other direction as I make these comments. I hope he can give us some information on this matter.

With regard to natural resource extraction, an orderly program of exploration and development of our lumber, mineral and water resources is required, along with assessment and exploration of oil and gas reserves. In respect of an over-all, co-ordinating program, adequate transportation systems must be developed. There must be a re-establishment of the roads to resources program. There must be a further development of rail facilities. There must be greater research into the transportation of oil and other resources from the high Arctic.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Panarctic is spending millions of dollars on exploratory work and many of these millions are public funds, but the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has indicated that he has not even thought of having research undertaken on how to transport oil from the high Arctic Islands if it is found in that area. That is rather startling when you consider the kind of expenditures being made. We still do not have any idea of how high Arctic oil will be taken to market so that a return may be realized on the investment.
There is some thought of a pipeline from the high Arctic, but there is no evidence that this is in fact a realistic mode of transportation, say of gas from Chris-

But it is a United States company that has done most of the research, with the Manhattan project, into this method of transportation. We are told that Baffin Island is the site of some of the world's largest iron ore deposits. It would appear that an initial investment of $150 million would provide sufficient capital to bring one of these deposits into production. Therefore, why is this deposit not being developed? Could it be because of the failure of this government to assume, wholly or in large part, the cost of providing the infrastructure facilities required to service an entire area?
It could be that the development of a government-sponsored Arctic shipping network could satisfy these requirements. It could be that construction of a modern townsite at Mary River-the site I referred to-would put to better use government funds now spent at Inuvik or Frobisher, where there is little or no industrial base and little to support the native peoples there except welfare.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude by again referring to the native population. I quote from the Globe and Mail of May 7 with respect to Indians in the Northwest Territories:
There is a growing feeling among Indian leaders in the Northwest Territories that Indians are being used as guinea pigs.
They feel that Indians have been overtaken with a subtle implementation of the basic concept of the federal government's supposedly discarded white paper Indian policy.
The basic concept of the white paper policy was to bring about integration of Indians into Canadian society by granting them equality through such measures as the abolition of the Indian Act and the disbanding of the Indian Affairs Department.
Indians reacted strongly against the policy proposal saying that it was simply a sop to white liberal ideals of equality which would result in the eradication of what remained of the rights granted to them for surrender of their land.
Again may I say that government policy which seeks to achieve healthy, productive and economically secure lives for the native peoples of Canada must respect their cultural heritage and traditions. The Canadian Indian must be free to choose to live in or away from his native community without prejudicing the opportunities available to him to enjoy the standard of living and quality of life of other Canadians. In both the formulation and application of such a policy the native peoples must be fully consulted and fully involved.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, thank you for your indulgence.
