subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-POTATOES-ASSISTANCE TO PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to pursue with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) on this adjournment debate a question of very great concern to the people of Prince
Edward Island. I am glad the minister is here this evening. This is an encouraging indication from him, I hope, of his interest and concern for the agricultural situation in Prince Edward Island.
I must confess quite frankly that from the answers the minister has given the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) and myself during the past few weeks I wondered whether he was either well informed or concerned about the very serious situation existing in respect of the agricultural industry in Prince Edward Island. For some weeks the hon. member for Malpeque and myself have been attempting to find out from the minister what forms of assistance his department envisaged in terms of the very real problems that exist in the potato industry in Prince Edward Island.
It is no secret to anyone acquainted with the marketing of potatoes over the past few years that for some years now we have experienced very depressed markets, particularly in the marketing of table-stock potatoes. As a result, a number of farmers have tried to diversify into other forms of agriculture or into the growing of seed potatoes. But we in Prince Edward Island are in a particularly distressing condition this year. That is why on Thursday of last week I asked the minister again-it was not a new question; it had been raised on a number of occasions-whether in view of the very depressed conditions of agriculture in PEI and the recent submissions by the provincial Minister of Agriculture, he was prepared to indicate what forms of assistance would be forthcoming to the potato growers as they faced heavy expense in buying fertilizer and seed.
As those involved in the industry know, there is a particularly distressing problem at the present time in terms of farmers having sufficient funds to be able to get on the land and engage in spring planting. There is the heavy expense-particularly so this year, I might say- involved in the purchase of seed because of a crop which was not altogether satisfactory last fall due to a damp period during harvesting, as well as disease, as a result of which the number of people who have usable seed this spring is smaller than usual. All this is an extra expense to PEI farmers. There is the added expense of fertilizer. With fertilizer, as with most of the costs relating to agriculture, there have been regular increases, I think particularly so during the last couple of years.
The minister's response to me last Thursday was simply to indicate that at the present time potatoes were going at a very high price. I was really shocked by this answer-shocked to think he would deal with the potato industry of Prince Edward Island in such a cavalier fashion. He must know, if he knows anything about the potato industry, that the number of farmers who would have any usable stock of potatoes for sale would be minimal, almost to the point of non-existence. For farmers, particularly this year, it was hard for them to hold stocks for any length of time and most had to sell their stocks last fall, during the winter or early in the spring. It was a shame for the minister to suggest that now that prices are somewhat higher this would be of assistance to the producers.

That is why on Monday I presented a motion in the House urging the government to consult immediately with the province of Prince Edward Island to formulate a program this week of immediate assistance. This should not have come as any great surprise. Indeed, the party presently in power, about three years ago-I believe when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) was Minister of Agriculture-initiated a program of acreage payments of, I think, $25 per acre which was of considerable assistance in terms of giving farmers sufficient financial resources with which to purchase badly needed seed and fertilizer.
I am wondering, Mr. Speaker-I do not really like to mention this-if we have not seen, because of the minister's unwillingness to act in this matter, a further instance of government policy to force a number of people to stop growing potatoes in Prince Edward Island. It is a rather brutal method, but I am told that one of the recommendations in a publication from his department suggests that there should be less potatoes grown this year. Well, that certainly will be the case so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, because already too many farmers have been driven to the point of bankruptcy or have had to sell off their farms by way of farm auction. I quote the words of one rural banker the other day when he said to me, in terms of the crisis into which too many farmers have been forced, "This is the worst I have ever seen."
When the minister quotes, as he did on Monday in reply to the hon. member for Malpeque, the long-term averages, when we look at the situation on the basis of long-term averages that really do not make the present situation look very serious, I suggest he is trying to divert attention away from the problem, particularly when he includes New Brunswick with PEI. I would remind the minister that the agricultural situation is very different, in terms of potatoes, between PEI and New Brunswick.

Mr. Speaker, as I previously advised the hon. member, I had a very useful meeting with the ministers of agriculture of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. At that time they submitted a formal proposal requesting assistance. The agricultural stabilization board, of course, have been considering the proposal and they have not closed out consideration of it, but there are a number of things we have to take into account.
While it is true that for a very short period the price of potatoes to producers dropped to a very low level, since then prices have strengthened significantly and are now higher than they have been in three of the last five years. I am sure the hon. member would be interested in noting that the estimated return to all growers in Canada for the 1970 crop year was approximately 90.4 per cent of the long-term average, and that Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick growers returns were 98.1 per cent and 94.8 per cent, respectively, of their long-term averages. The return to the producers in Prince Edward Island, as a percentage of the long-term average, was higher than any other province for the 1970 crop year.
I do not wish to comment on the problems that agricultural producers are having with respect to purchasing seed, fertilizer and so on. I am sure the hon. member realizes that when we initiate an assistance program we must take into account the total returns to producers from their crops.
